The movement of the determinists, or Jahmiyya, played an important role in the development of Arab thought toward rational and philosophical inquiry. Its influence was no less important than that of the Qadarite movement, even though the doctrine of compulsion itself carried what we regard as a negative ideological meaning.
Like the Qadarites, the determinists also relied on reason to explain and defend their views.
Both groups, after all, belonged to the same general Islamic intellectual framework.

For this reason, we can say that the Jahmiyya also played an active part in laying some of the earliest foundations for the rational movement that would eventually lead Arab thought toward philosophy.
Our study of the determinist movement dealt with several questions that formed the main elements of its doctrine:
D — Whether reason can know good and evil
E — Whether God can be seen
According to al-Shahrastānī’s account, Jahm ibn Ṣafwān’s theory of compulsion holds that human beings have no power of their own and cannot truly be described as capable of acting.
They are compelled in their actions.
They possess no real power, will, or choice. Instead, God creates actions in human beings just as He creates events in other inanimate things.
Actions are therefore attributed to human beings only figuratively, not in the true sense, just as actions may figuratively be attributed to inanimate objects.
Jahm does not deny that human beings appear different from inanimate things because we speak of them as having will and choice.
But he says that “in reality no one acts except God alone, and He is the true agent.”
This leaves the human qualities of will and choice with no real function or effect.
Human will becomes something mechanical. It no longer carries the true meaning of will.
Yet despite the absolute and deeply negative determinism of this theory, Jahm takes the side of reason in several other questions.

In dealing with those questions, he uses a form of philosophical reasoning. He also helps open a rational path that later thinkers—especially the Muʿtazilites and the theologians of kalām—would continue to develop.
This is the first question in which we said that Jahm takes the side of reason.
Here he gives rational judgment priority over the apparent meaning of Qurʾanic texts.
He denies that God possesses attributes separate from His essence, even though the surface meaning of some Qurʾanic passages may seem to suggest otherwise.
His starting point is the principle that God must not be made similar to human beings, whose qualities and attributes are many.
Jahm therefore turns to rational argument and works with abstract concepts.
This placed him in opposition to the anthropomorphists, who were unable to think about divinity at the level of abstract concepts and meanings and instead imagined God in a concrete and bodily form.
Jahm’s denial of separate divine attributes also led him to say that the Qurʾan was created rather than being the eternal speech of God.
So on both the question of the divine attributes and the created Qurʾan, Jahm anticipated positions later associated with the Muʿtazilites.
Here too, Jahm introduced a bold and unusual position that went against the apparent meaning of Qurʾanic texts.
He denied that the world of the afterlife would last forever.

He argued that the activity of the inhabitants of both eternal abodes—Paradise and Hell—would eventually come to an end, and that Paradise and Hell themselves would cease to exist after their inhabitants had entered them.
He based this view on a philosophical argument: an infinite chain of movements stretching endlessly backward or forward cannot be conceived.
For Jahm, then, motion is neither eternal in the past nor endless in the future.
He applied this understanding of motion to the afterlife, which he appears to have treated by analogy with the material world.
For the same reason, he argued that God had not yet created Paradise. The Paradise of Adam mentioned in the religious texts, he said, had been created by God and then brought to an end.
D — Whether Reason Can Know Good and Evil
This is another question in which Jahm anticipated later Muʿtazilite and kalām thinkers.
Here his reliance on reason becomes even clearer.
He treats reason as capable of discovering what is good or bad, beneficial or harmful, in things, actions, the different forms of existence, and ideas themselves.
Jahm therefore held that reason can recognize the goodness or badness of things on its own, even before divine law reveals them.
On this basis, he argued for “the obligation of knowledge through reason before revelation.”
In other words, reason itself makes it necessary for human beings to know God even before revelation gives them that command.
This means that Jahm’s theory of knowledge does not depend first of all on a divine source. It begins with reason.
This is an important progressive element in his thought.

There is another progressive element as well. Jahm treats goodness and badness as qualities that exist objectively in things themselves. Their basic character does not depend on the prior existence of divine law.
E — Whether God Can Be Seen
Jahm denies that God can be seen in the afterlife.
This went against the position of the traditionalists, who based their view on Qurʾanic texts.

They also used a rational argument that can be stated like this: everything that exists can be seen; anything that cannot be seen cannot be proven to exist; since God’s existence has been established, it must therefore be possible to see Him.
We described this as a rational argument because it is built from rational premises.
It also has the form of a logical argument of the kind associated with Aristotelian formal logic.
This suggests that organized rational reasoning was already beginning to impose itself even on conservative traditionalists.
We mention this here only in passing, but it has important historical meaning.

He denied absolutely that God could be seen, either in this world or in the afterlife. This followed from his earlier denial of separate divine attributes and his rejection of any comparison between God and created beings.
He answered the argument of the traditionalists—including the Ashʿarites—by saying that its premises cannot be applied to God.
God, he argued, is “not a thing.”
He therefore does not fall under the premise that “everything that exists can be seen,” because an existent thing, in the sense intended by that premise, is a “thing.”
Although Jahm’s argument here has a metaphysical direction, it also shows an abstract way of thinking about the nature of God.
This represents a higher level of theoretical awareness.
In this respect, Jahm comes closer to philosophical thought than the traditionalists do.
Here again, Jahm anticipated questions that the Muʿtazilites and Ashʿarites would later debate in much greater detail.
He denied that God’s knowledge is eternal, despite the apparent meaning of Qurʾanic texts. Instead, he held that God’s knowledge comes into being.
At the same time, Jahm could not simply deny knowledge to God.

He therefore turned the problem into a philosophical one and eventually reached the conclusion that God’s knowledge has no particular location and is not one single, universal body of knowledge embracing everything at once.
His knowledge is therefore multiple to the same extent that individual things themselves are multiple.
With this conclusion, Jahm laid part of the foundation for a later dispute among the theologians of kalām, both Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite: Does God know only universals? Only particulars? Or both?
What matters for us here is the way Jahm formulated the problem and the way he tried to solve it.
Our examination of his position showed that this determinist thinker relied on a rational method that already had something of the character of philosophical thought.
In particular, he used logical and philosophical concepts and categories in dealing with the question.
Jahm also introduced a new definition of faith.
Two different definitions had already existed before him.
The traditionalist definition held that faith consists of belief in God and His messengers, followed by openly declaring that belief.
The Khārijites added a third element: action in accordance with what belief requires.
We regarded Jahm’s new definition as a further development in the Islamic understanding of faith.
For him, faith consists of only one thing: knowledge.
By this he means knowledge of God, His messengers, and His laws.
Nothing else forms part of faith itself.

“If a person comes to knowledge and then denies it with his tongue, that denial does not make him an unbeliever. Knowledge and understanding are not removed by verbal denial, so he remains a believer.”
For Jahm, this also means that faith cannot be divided into belief, speech, and action.
Nor is one person superior to another in the degree of his faith.
The faith of the prophets and the faith of ordinary members of the community are of the same kind, because knowledge itself does not admit of such degrees.
If this is what Jahm means by faith, what does he mean by unbelief?
“Unbelief is one single quality. It belongs to the heart, and it is ignorance of God.”
This is also reported by al-Ashʿarī in Maqālāt, vol. 1, p. 128.
But if knowledge is faith, what kind of knowledge does Jahm mean?
We should remember that he treats rational knowledge as the first path to God, even before revealed law.
The knowledge he means in his definition of faith must therefore be rational knowledge.
Here we can see that Jahm represents a new way of thinking.

At this stage in the history of Arab-Islamic thought, his approach brings us to the beginning of a major turning point: the movement toward the rational method of the theologians of kalām, which would in turn help prepare the way for the emergence of philosophy.
